title: Ceramic Tile Grout Calculator 2026 — kg/m² | Hacé Cuentas
description: Calculate exactly how many kg of grout you need for any ceramic, porcelain, or mosaic tile job. Uses the real industry formula: tile size, joint width, tile thickness, and waste margin.
intro:
The Ceramic Tile Grout Calculator estimates the exact kilograms of grout needed to fill all joints in a given tiled surface area. Instead of a generic lookup table, it uses the authoritative industry formula published by manufacturers such as Mapei and Weber: **kg/m² = [(L + W) / (L × W)] × J × T × ρ** — where L and W are tile dimensions in mm, J is joint width in mm, T is tile thickness (which equals joint depth), and ρ is the dry bulk density of the grout (≈ 1.70 kg/dm³ for standard cement-based products).

The formula accounts for the key insight that smaller tiles produce far more linear joint per square meter than large-format tiles: a 20×20 cm grid has roughly 10 m of joint per m², while a 60×60 cm grid has only 3.3 m/m². Combined with joint width and depth, this directly drives the kg/m² figure.

Use this calculator before purchasing materials for any floor, wall, pool surround, or countertop ceramic tiling project. Enter the surface area, tile size, joint width, tile thickness, and your desired waste margin (10% for standard work, 15% for complex layouts or exterior use). The calculator returns the unit consumption (kg/m²) and the total quantity to buy, with bag size suggestions based on common pack sizes (1, 2, 5, 20 kg).
keyTakeaway: **kg/m² = [(L + W) / (L × W)] × J × T × 1.70** — e.g., 30×30 cm tile (300×300 mm), 3 mm joint, 8 mm thick: 0.272 kg/m². Over 20 m² with 10% waste = **5.98 kg total**.

Estimating grout quantity for a 90 m² commercial floor using large-format 60×60 cm porcelain tiles at 1.5 mm joints to submit an accurate materials budget (result: ≈ 8.4 kg).
Planning grout purchases for a 35 m² outdoor patio using rustic 20×20 cm tiles at 6 mm joints where a 15% waste margin applies (result: ≈ 41 kg).

explanation:
## How It Is Calculated

The authoritative formula for ceramic tile grout consumption (published by Mapei, Weber, and Sika) is:

```
kg/m² = [(L + W) / (L × W)] × J × T × ρ

Where (all lengths in mm):
  L = Tile length (mm)
  W = Tile width (mm)
  J = Joint width (mm)
  T = Tile thickness / joint depth (mm)
  ρ = Grout bulk density (kg/dm³)
      ≈ 1.70 kg/dm³ for standard cement-based grout

Total with waste:
  kg_total = kg/m² × Area_m² × (1 + waste_% / 100)
```

**Unit proof:**
- (L+W)/(L×W) → 1/mm
- × J (mm) × T (mm) → mm (joint cross-section volume per mm² of surface)
- × 1,000,000 mm²/m² ÷ 1,000,000 mm³/dm³ = dm³/m²
- × ρ (kg/dm³) → kg/m² ✓

**Worked example:**
- Tile 30×30 cm (300×300 mm), joint 3 mm, thickness 8 mm, area 20 m²
- kg/m² = [(300+300)/(300×300)] × 3 × 8 × 1.70 = 0.00667 × 40.8 = **0.272 kg/m²**
- Total = 0.272 × 20 × 1.10 = **5.98 kg** → 1×5 kg bag + 1×1 kg bag

---

*Values exclude waste. Add 10% for standard work, 15% for complex layouts or exterior use.*

---

## Common Mistakes

1. **Skipping the waste factor:** On-site cutting, spillage, and re-mixing typically consume an additional 8–15%. Always add at least 10%.

2. **Confusing joint width with joint depth:** Width is the visible gap between tiles (e.g., 3 mm); depth is how far the grout penetrates (equals tile thickness). Using only width underestimates the joint volume and leads to under-purchasing.

3. **Ignoring tile size:** At the same joint width, a 20×20 cm tile generates nearly twice as many meters of joint per m² as a 40×40 cm tile — requiring proportionally more grout.

4. **Mixing up grout densities:** Epoxy grout (used in wet areas and food-prep surfaces) has a density of ≈ 1.4 kg/dm³, lower than cement-based (1.70 kg/dm³). Using the wrong density can overestimate quantity by 20%.

5. **Mixing too much at once:** Cement grout has a working time of 20–30 minutes. Plan batch sizes of 2–3 kg at a time for DIY work to avoid hardened waste.

faq.q: What is the exact formula for calculating how much grout I need?
faq.a: The industry-standard formula is: kg/m² = [(L + W) / (L × W)] × J × T × ρ. Here L and W are tile length and width in mm, J is joint width in mm, T is tile thickness in mm (which equals joint depth), and ρ is grout bulk density — approximately 1.70 kg/dm³ for standard cement-based products from brands like Mapei, Weber, or Laticrete. Multiply by your surface area in m² and add 10% for waste to get the total to purchase.

faq.q: Why does tile size affect grout consumption so significantly?
faq.a: Grout consumption is driven by the total linear length of joints per square meter. Smaller tiles have far more joints per m² than large-format tiles. A 20×20 cm tile grid has roughly 10 m of joint per m² of floor, while a 60×60 cm grid has only 3.3 m/m². Since grout fills the full width and depth of each joint, smaller tiles require proportionally much more grout — often 3–6× more per m² compared to large-format tiles at the same joint width.

faq.q: What waste margin should I add to the calculated grout quantity?
faq.a: The industry standard is a minimum of 10% waste for straightforward rectangular rooms with few cuts. For complex layouts (diagonal patterns, curved walls, mosaic work), increase to 15%. For epoxy grout — which is expensive and must be mixed precisely — 10% is standard, but avoid over-purchasing since unused mixed epoxy cannot be returned or stored.

faq.q: What is the difference between sanded and unsanded grout, and when should I use each?
faq.a: Unsanded grout is used for joints under 3 mm wide; it is smooth enough to avoid scratching polished or glazed tile surfaces. Sanded grout contains fine sand aggregate and is required for joints 3 mm or wider — the sand prevents shrinkage cracking as the grout cures. Per ANSI A108.10, using unsanded grout in joints wider than 3 mm results in surface cracking within 1–2 years due to shrinkage stress.

faq.q: Can I use this calculator for porcelain or natural stone tiles, not just ceramics?
faq.a: Yes — the formula applies to any rigid tile material including porcelain, natural stone (marble, slate, travertine), glass tiles, and cement-look tiles. The key variable is tile thickness: natural stone tiles are often thicker (10–15 mm) than standard ceramics (6–9 mm), which increases grout volume. For glass tiles, always use unsanded or epoxy grout to avoid scratching the surface.

faq.q: How do I calculate grout for a wall versus a floor — is there any difference?
faq.a: The formula and factors are identical for both floor and wall applications. The main practical difference is joint width convention: wall tiles traditionally use narrower joints (1.5–2 mm) with unsanded grout for a cleaner aesthetic finish, while floor tiles often use 3–5 mm joints for leveling tolerance. Always measure the actual wall surface area excluding windows, doors, and fixtures, and apply the same waste factor regardless of orientation.

faq.q: Is epoxy grout calculated the same way as cement grout?
faq.a: The volume calculation is the same, but epoxy grout has a lower density (approximately 1.4 kg/dm³ vs. 1.70 kg/dm³ for cement grout), so the kg quantity is about 18% less for the same joint volume. Epoxy grout is also sold in pre-measured two-part kits (resin + hardener) rather than loose bags, so you purchase by kit coverage area. Epoxy is required in commercial food-preparation surfaces per food safety codes and strongly recommended for swimming pools.

faq.q: How long does mixed grout remain workable, and can I store leftover dry grout bags?
faq.a: Mixed cement-based grout must be used within 20–30 minutes of preparation — it cannot be stored once water is added. Unmixed dry grout bags, kept sealed in a cool, dry location, typically have a shelf life of 12–24 months. Always check the expiration date on the bag before use; expired grout may have reduced strength and poor water resistance after curing.

faq.q: What happens if the grout joint is too narrow or too wide?
faq.a: A joint under 1.5 mm makes complete filling very difficult, leaves internal voids, and can crack quickly because it cannot accommodate thermal expansion and contraction of the tiles. An excessively wide joint (over 10 mm) without flexibility additives can crack at the center due to shrinkage during curing. For joints over 10 mm, mix fine washed sand into the grout or use a structural joint mortar formulated for that width.

faq.q: Does grout color affect consumption or coverage?
faq.a: Grout color does not meaningfully affect consumption per square meter, since the base formulation is the same across colors. Grouts with intense pigments (black, deep blue) may have a slightly higher density — typically 3–5% more — which is negligible in practice. What matters is buying all grout for a large surface from the same manufacturing batch to avoid color variation between bags, especially for special or custom colors that may not always be in stock.

faq.q: When should I use epoxy grout instead of cement-based grout?
faq.a: Epoxy grout is the right choice when chemical resistance, impermeability, or extreme durability are priorities: swimming pools, jacuzzis, saunas, commercial kitchens, laboratories, or any area permanently exposed to aggressive detergents, acids, or grease. It is also recommended under very heavy traffic or mechanical loads. The downsides are cost (5–10× more per kg than cement), more complex application (precise two-part mixing, shorter working time), and difficulty removing if it dries on the tile face. For standard domestic interiors, high-quality cement-based grout is fully sufficient.
